Prepared: March 2023 Self-Study of the URI Honors Program R UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND PROGRAM DIRECTOR:KAREN DE BRUIN

I would like to thank the Oﬃce of the Provost for aﬀording us the opportunity to conduct a self study and external review of the URI Honors Program.
Through this process of self-study, using the “NCHC Program Review Instrument,” we have been able to learn in depth the best practices of mature honors programs.
This report constitutes the ﬁrst formal self study of our URI Honors Program conducted for external review.
Prior to this 2023 report, there were two other self-studies that provide useful historical information regarding the evolution of URI “Honors”: a 2013 informal self-study and a 2005 study of the relationship between the Scholarship Oﬃce and the Honors Program.
Due to an evolution that is speciﬁc to the resource allocation history at the University of Rhode Island, “URI Honors'' is actually comprised of four distinct entities: the Honors Program; the Honors Colloquium; the Oﬃce of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities; and the Pre-Health Professions Advising Program.
The Honors Colloquium will celebrate its sixtieth anniversary in Fall 2023.

The Colloquium spawned the URI Honors Program, roughly forty years ago, and it was about twenty years ago that the Honors Program took its current form.
While advising for national fellowships existed informally within the Honors Program, in 2013, Honors formalized fellowship advising with the creation of an Oﬃce of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities (ONFAO).
This oﬃce also conducted pre-health advising until 2016, when fellowships advising was formally uncoupled from pre-health advising. (Honors took over Pre-health advising from the College of the Environment and Life Sciences in 2009.) Currently, one person is staﬃng the ONFAO and serving as its director.
She also served as the pre-health advisor until the position was uncoupled from national fellowships advising.
Pre-health has both a director and a half-time advisor line, currently ﬁlled with an interim advisor.
This report is designed to be read alongside the NCHC Program Review Instrument, which provides a rubric for evaluation for honors programs and colleges.

Since this self-study has been scaﬀolded by the NCHC Program Review Instrument, which is dedicated speciﬁcally to Honors Program education, it will primarily present reﬂections on and evaluations of the URI Honors Program.
For reviewer consideration, we have included in the Appendix a Pre-health Professions Advising Program self-study as well as the last annual report of the ONFAO.
The Honors Program is currently at a juncture of change.
In the past year, the previous director of the program, Lynne Derbyshire, retired after nine years of service to the program; the Honors Program Coordinator of thirty-seven years, Deborah Gardiner, also retired; and the half-time continuing pre-health advisor left.
The departures of both Lynne Derbyshire and, especially, Deborah Gardiner have left an information gap that we are struggling to ﬁll.
Coupled with these departures will be the exiting of two (of three) associate directors – Kathleen McIntyre, who will be

returning to Gender & Women’s Studies; and Smita Ramnarain, whose one-year sabbatical next year will coincide with the last year of her term.
The term of Jill Doerner, the remaining associate director, is also ending in spring 2023.
At the macro level, the University welcomed a new President, Marc Parlange, in Fall 2021 and a new Provost, Barbara Wolfe, in January of 2023.
It also rolled out a new Strategic Plan in 2023.
And in September 2022, I stepped in as the new director of the Honors Program, charged with bringing strategic vision.
This report thus represents our Honors Program at a locus of transition.
It presents and evaluates the program as it was, based on the history that we have available to us, with an eye to where we are heading.
There are a number of key takeaway points that we highlight throughout this study in textboxes and quotes.
Below I call attention to two of the most salient ones: ●The Honors Program is a key recruitment and retention tool for the University in order to attract high-achieving students, thereby enhancing the University’s student population, proﬁle of its graduates, and quality of its alumni.

Over the past ﬁfteen years, the program has grown tremendously in terms of incoming Honors-eligible freshmen, reaching almost 1,500 incoming eligible Honors students, or one third of the admitted freshman class.
In the last ﬁve years alone, we have seen a thirty-six percent increase in the number of Honors-eligible students.
Roughly 1,000 of these 1,500 Honors-eligible students seek seats in Honors courses their ﬁrst semester of college.
The focus in the past has been to provide a multitude of 100- and 200-level courses that fulﬁll General Education requirements so that as many ﬁrst- and second-year Honors-eligible students as possible can experience the intimate, high-impact nature of the Honors curriculum, thereby enhancing retention of top-performing ﬁrst- and second-year students. ●The Honors Program as it currently exists is unsustainable The unsustainability of the Honors Program as it currently exists is rooted in a number of factors including unmet student expectations; an unclear mission; a lack of programmatic goals; no assessment or evaluation processes and procedures; an opaque budget structure; funding limitations; and major structural challenges.

The goal of this self-study and external review is to produce a strategic plan, to be presented to and approved by the President and the Provost, that will guide the Honors Program and resource allocation for the program over the next ﬁve years.
The new strategic direction of Honors is already sketched and can be found in the Appendix as a presentation entitled“New Strategic Direction.”We refer to our “new strategic direction” often in this report.

We are very excited about our new strategic direction, which is organized both around the mission of “Imagining Sustainable, Equitable Societies” and the most visible and distinguishing centerpiece of Honors: our Honors Colloquium.
Our students and our children are facing unparalleled challenges –

climate change, biodiversity collapse, irreversible pollution, looming food instability, declining democracy, mass migrations, a rising reign of artiﬁcial intelligence, and maybe even nuclear war.
It is essential that they go forth into their professional lives knowingwhat they can do.
The Honors Colloquium has typically tackled these challenges yearly with nationally, and sometimes internationally, renowned speakers.

We would like to build on the Colloquium by structuring our Honors Program around stackable Honors Certiﬁcates that provide real-world experiential learning around themes like: sustainable, equitable food systems; sustaining our shores; business for the common good; resilient, equitable democracies; sustainable design; and sustainable, equitable healthcare. (Almost all of these themes are either prior or future Colloquium topics with interested faculty members and deans already sketching the contours of these future “certiﬁcates.”) We believe that this new structure of Honors will not only distinguish our URI Honors Program from Honors programs and colleges at peer institutions but it will also attract serious changemakers, leaders and activists, and provide them with the tools to become the engaged citizens that we need.
This new structure will also allow us to build on existing academic strengths of the University of Rhode Island and to launch certiﬁcates that can become campus-wide after their initial pilot runs in Honors.

According to theNCHC Program Review Instrument, amature Honors Program “is a permanent and highly regarded unit that contributes centrally and substantially to the overall traditions of excellence on campus.” The history of Honors at the University of Rhode Island has provided us with a robust foundation from which we can grow.
